I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00213

Like almost all Iranian scholars of his time, he wrote not only in Arabic, the “liturgical language,” but also in Persian. And he would hardly have been a true Iranian scholar had he not also been a poet. Rezâ Qolî Hedâyat mentions a mathnawî, a poem in rhyming couplets, of his composition called Mashriq al-Anwâr (“The Orient of Lights”). It is fair to say that no branch of Islamic learning was foreign to him.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00214

In short, he emerges as a profound thinker with an extraordinary capacity for work, driven by an energy and a demand for self-discipline that approached austerity. His pupils were devoted enough to spend years commenting on his work, and his humanity shines through the lifelong friendship that united him with Bahâ'oddîn 'Âmilî. These two facts speak most eloquently for the man himself.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00215

We should add that he possessed a sense of humor, as certain anecdotes show. His biographers agree in emphasizing his fervent devotion, his intense spiritual practice, and the mystical disposition that could carry him into ecstasy—as the brief confessions translated later in this chapter convincingly attest. Such was the man who deserved to be called Mo'allim-e thâlîth, Magister tertius, the Third Teacher. Unfortunately, apart from two or three books, the publication of his works has so far been neglected. It is almost as though the writings of his most famous disciple, Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî—read, reread, and commented upon by generation after generation of Iranian philosophers—had partly eclipsed those of the master.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00216

To place Mîr Dâmâd within his spiritual family, we should now recall his teachers and pupils, the connections leading to and from each of them—in short, recover and follow further the web woven by their thoughts and souls. As we have said, there is no prior research on which we can draw to make even the beginning of this work easier. The man who, through his pupils and their pupils in turn, would dominate the religious philosophy of Iran over the next four centuries had first studied under his maternal uncle, Shaykh 'Abd al-'Âlî (926/1520–993/1585), and Shaykh 'Izzoddîn Hosayn ibn 'Abd al-Samad (912/1506–1507 to 984/1576–1577), the father of Shaykh-e Bahâ'î, who was to become his lifelong friend and brother in spirit.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00217

Two other teachers united in themselves the twin Illuminationist and Shiite traditions. One was Mîr Fakhroddîn Mohammad Samâkî Astarâbâdî, who had himself studied under Mîr Giyâthoddîn Mansûr Shîrâzî (d. 949/1548), a renowned philosopher and commentator on Sohrawardî’s Temples of Light. The other was Sayyed Nûroddîn 'Alî ibn Abî'l-Hasan al-'Âmilî, a pupil of Shaykh Zaynoddîn al-'Âmilî (911/1505–1506 to 966/1558–1559), known among the Imamites as the “Second Martyr” (Shahîd-e thânî).
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00218

Thus, both by spiritual inheritance and by family descent, Mîr Dâmâd received the most authentic Shiite heritage. At the same time, he inherited Sohrawardî’s ishrâq—if not every particular philosophical thesis advanced by the Master of Illumination, then at least the spiritual “orientation” he had given to philosophical inquiry. We have already emphasized how this joining of traditions characterizes Iranian philosophy under the Safavids and also under the Qajars, whose most distinguished representatives include Mollâ Hâdî Sabzavârî (d. 1878).
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00219

This union, embodied in Mîr Dâmâd, continued through his pupils. We shall mention only a few. There are secondary figures, such as Hosayn ibn Haydar Karakî, the moftî of Isfahan (d. 1029 AH), and 'Âdil Morâd Ârdastânî.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00220

But towering above them, with a fame beyond comparison, is Sadroddîn Shîrâzî (Mollâ Sadrâ), who would die barely ten years after his teacher (1050/1640–1641). What Mîr Dâmâd had been to Isfahan, Mollâ Sadrâ became to Shiraz, where it is still possible to sit in quiet reflection in the small room in which he once gave his lessons. We have referred to him repeatedly in the preceding pages. As we shall recall in the chapter devoted to him, his work dominates the entire Iranian philosophical tradition of the past four centuries, and a revival of traditional philosophy in Iran is now taking shape around it.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00221

Another figure, less famous but no less engaging, is Sayyed Ahmad ibn Zayn al-'Âbidîn 'Alawî (d. around 1054–1060/1644–1650). He was Mîr Dâmâd’s own cousin, the son of his maternal aunt. He became his pupil and then his son-in-law, but above all he was, and remained, his “spiritual child” (walad rûhânî), as Mîr Dâmâd calls him in one of the formal authorizations (Ijâzât) he granted him.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00222

As I have gradually reconstructed his writings, I have come to recognize their importance for the structure of Iranian Shiite Avicennianism, and his major role in interpreting his master’s thought. He deserves a monograph of his own and would naturally occupy a prominent place in any comprehensive account of our School of Isfahan. The title of his great commentary on Avicenna, The Key to the Shifâ, is especially revealing, for it presents “Oriental philosophy” itself as that key.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00223
Beside Mollâ Sadrâ and our Sayyed stands a whole procession of pupils and followers.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00224

Let us name a few more. Mollâ Khalîl Qazwînî (1001/1592–1089/1681) wrote a substantial and very useful Persian commentary on Kolaynî’s Osûl min al-Kâfî, one of the four foundational books of Shiism, to which we have already referred. All the commentaries on this work ought to be studied side by side.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00225

Yet Mollâ Sadrâ’s philosophical commentary, though unfinished, surpasses them all in breadth of thought. The poet Mohammad Hasan Zalâlî (d. around 1031/1622) composed, in imitation of Nizâmî and Jâmî, a collection of seven mathnawî poems. Special mention must be made of Qotboddîn Mohammad Ashkevarî, who composed an immense kind of rhapsody in Arabic and Persian.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00226

In three parts, it assembles traditions, quotations, and commentaries concerning the ancient sages; the philosophers and spiritual masters of Sunni Islam; and finally the Imams and great spiritual figures of Shiism. It is a kind of speculum historiale, a historical mirror of “divine philosophy,” the Divinalia, beginning with Adam and ending with the author’s own master, Mîr Dâmâd. In the chapter devoted to him, Ashkevarî reproduces in full the two ecstatic confessions translated later in this work.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00227

Of course, this immediate circle around Mîr Dâmâd by no means exhausts the history of the School of Isfahan. We would also have to name the great pupils of Mollâ Sadrâ, such as Mohsen-e Fayz and 'Abdorrazzâq Lâhîjî; and Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, who comments on Ibn Bâbûyeh’s Kitâb al-Tawhîd as a true master of gnosis and stands beside Mollâ Sadrâ as one of the indispensable authorities for any study of Shiite mystical knowledge. A later chapter is devoted to him.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00228

The school of Mollâ Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî, whose pupil Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî was, remains almost entirely unknown: Mohammad Rafî'â, Shamsâ Gîlânî, and others. Nor have all these names yet brought us to the crucial fact of the age, already mentioned in discussing the Illuminationist tradition (Book II, Chapter VII): the extraordinary movement back and forth between Iran and India prompted by Shah Akbar’s generous religious reform. One great traveler, Mîr Abû'l-Qâsim Fendereskî, is named in the translations then being made from Sanskrit into Persian.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00229

As an instance of spiritual traditions entering into one another, this undertaking can be compared to the translation of Greek works into Syriac and Arabic, or Arabic works into Latin, yet it has scarcely been studied. It was during this same period, as we have said—at the turn of our sixteenth and seventeenth centuries—that a whole group of Zoroastrians from Shiraz migrated to India with their high priest, Azar Kayvân.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00230

Among them, Sohrawardî’s work found understanding and even devotion, as in the case of Farzanah Bahrâm, answering the very intention with which it had been written: to “revive the wisdom of ancient Persia.” These Zoroastrians recognized their own inheritance in the wisdom of Ishrâq. It was also at this time, in 1008/1599–1600, that Mohammad Sharîf ibn Harawî, an Iranian deeply familiar with Indian Sufism, translated the Book of Oriental Theosophy from Arabic into Persian. Through all this devotion and inquiry, and through the wounds and anxieties of the age, we come at last to the close of our eighteenth century and the emergence of the Shaykhi school with Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î—a living witness to the metaphysical and spiritual possibilities contained in Shiism (see Book VI below).
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00231
Mîr Dâmâd’s name has thus led us to evoke a long procession of sages, philosophers, theologians, and mystics. It may be said that what we have offered is a program for future research. Certainly.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00232

But setting it out at least justifies the complaint we echoed earlier. We are dealing with an entire spiritual culture whose great works await the philosopher and researcher. They call for the long, demanding labor of examining and thinking them through anew, until a whole region, a whole spiritual “style,” finally becomes present on the horizon of our consciousness. Its absence is a paradox and an impoverishment that harms us all. Several signs allow us to believe that this other jâhilîya, this “age of ignorance,” is drawing to a close.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00233

To conclude our account of Mîr Dâmâd’s work, his pupils, and his successors, I shall mention a work of extraordinary size, exceeding even Mollâ Sadrâ’s great philosophical Summa, the Asfâr arba'a. It is a commentary on Mîr Dâmâd’s Qabasât, written by Mohammad ibn 'Alî Rezâ ibn Âqâjânî Mazandarânî, a figure I have so far been unable to trace anywhere else.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00234

Here we can only say that he completed it in 1071/1661 and that he was a pupil of Mollâ Sadrâ and probably of Mîr Dâmâd as well. A marginal note found in a related manuscript specifies that although he had studied under Mollâ Sadrâ, he did not follow him in his doctrine of the transcendent unity of being (wahdat al-wojûd). How many years of his life must this pupil have devoted to erecting so vast a Summa upon one of his master’s principal works—a work that was itself a monument of Shiite Avicennianism!
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd

2. Vision in the Mosque of Qom
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00235

Once again, we have used the expression “Shiite Avicennianism,” for it seems immediately appropriate not only to the thought and writings of Mîr Dâmâd but also to the entire body of inquiry that grew up around them. Certainly, as we have noted, this tradition contains many shades of opinion and many different philosophical positions. More often than not, its Avicennianism bears an Illuminationist coloring, even when our thinkers reject one or another doctrine associated with Sohrawardî’s line of thought.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00236

Consider, for example, the crucial question of the imaginal world ('âlam mithâlî), the intermediate realm of spiritual images. Mollâ Sadrâ took a firm position on this question, affirming the “separate,” immaterial nature (tajarrod) both of the imaginal world and of Imagination as the faculty through which that intermediate world is perceived. Mîr Dâmâd does not accept the thesis of the imaginal world’s immateriality in this form; yet his argument includes the idea of an “imaginal matter,” which ultimately leads back to the perception of the very reality under discussion.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00237

The delicate task is therefore to weigh exactly what each side means when it accepts or rejects the transcendence or immateriality of the imaginal, of the intermediate world called barzakh. Mîr Dâmâd the philosopher knew perfectly well what the reality of the world of visions implies. An Avicennian whose personal philosophy culminates in a visionary perception of the kind attested by the second ecstatic confession translated below is an Avicennian who has learned from Sohrawardî.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00238

An Avicennian whose mystical experience flowers into a vision of the presence of the Prophet and the Imams is a Shiite Avicennian, as the account of Mîr Dâmâd’s vision in the mosque of Qom shows us. And that such visionary perception presupposes the spiritual teaching of Ishrâq is something Mîr Dâmâd himself confirms, by quoting at just the right moment a few lines from one of Sohrawardî’s most characteristic pages.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00239

In short, this type of Shiite spiritual thinker deserves to be called ishrâqî, Illuminationist, because it decisively refutes an opposition too commonly assumed, and one we have already had reason to deplore: the supposed incompatibility between the most abstract philosophical speculation and the intimate devotion of the heart, between rigorous thought and an inner life so intense that it reaches genuine mystical experience. To maintain this opposition, one must hold a conception of philosophy fundamentally opposed to that of Sohrawardî and all those who share it, whether or not they call themselves Ishrâqîyûn. Some, for example, dispute the legitimacy of interpreting philosophically a mystical rhapsody such as the Mathnawî of Mawlânâ Jalâloddîn Rûmî.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00240

But anyone who does so certainly understands philosophy very differently from these spiritual masters. What they regard as the very purpose and culmination of philosophical meditation flatly contradicts the claim that philosophy and mystical capacity cannot coexist. Since philosophical meditation stands at the threshold of the Way, it always remains possible, in the light of the Way’s successive stages, to recognize earlier moments and states as so many illuminations that first guided the traveler onto it.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00241

Let us recall once again that Sohrawardî’s Oriental Theosophy begins with a reform of logic and ends with a reminder of ecstasy. In exactly the same way, Mîr Dâmâd’s extraordinarily difficult philosophical writings reach their summit in the lived states whose traces are preserved forever in the two accounts presented below. Of the second account we may say that it employs the technical vocabulary of Avicenna’s metaphysics of being, but that Avicennianism bursts beyond its own limits and ends far above itself. Even so, its Avicennian vocabulary attests full awareness of what preceded and made possible the emergence of the mystical vision. These echoes help us place both “ecstatic confessions” within the larger setting of Mîr Dâmâd’s teaching.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00242

We owe the idea of collecting these two accounts together to Qotboddîn Ashkevarî. With a remarkable gift for arranging and weaving texts together, he brought into one sequence some of his master’s most revealing writings. What emerges is not a summary of theoretical teaching, but a spiritual personality appearing in flashes of light through these few texts. One of them comes from the conclusion of a book dealing with a precise point of religious law (Kitâb zawâbit al-rizâ')—hardly the kind of work in which one would think to look for a mystical narrative.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00243

But this is Mîr Dâmâd. The seal he places upon his treatise reveals his distinctive style and his mastery of ta'wîl, spiritual interpretation: his capacity to transform everything into symbols. A human being, he explains, is a recapitulation (fadhlakat) of the hierarchy of worlds, belonging to two orders of existence at once.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00244

Through the “temple” (haykal) of the material, organic body, the human being belongs to the world of physical nature; through the thinking essence, the independent and immaterial soul (mojarrada), the human being belongs to the spiritual or angelic world. This is no harmless proposition of theoretical philosophy. It carries with it the necessity of a double birth and a double “nursing” (rizâ'), one in the sensible world and the other in the spiritual world. To be born into the spiritual world—one’s birth “in the true sense” (wilâdat haqîqîya)—the human being, as a spiritual child, must be nourished by the light of knowledge and the beauty of wisdom.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00245

Now just as physical nursing (rizâ' jasadânî) legally establishes a kinship comparable to that arising from birth and has consequences and fruits in the order of life to which that birth belongs, so spiritual nursing (rizâ' rûhânî) creates a kinship belonging to the lineage of the spirit: an ancestry leading back to the communities of the angelic world. In that realm, too, it bears consequences and fruits. These are union with the holy, intelligible Lights, with the surpassing beauty of the archangels of the highest rank (moqarrabûn), and with the innumerable angelic communities.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00246

Above all, it is union with the Holy Spirit (Rûh al-Qods), the Giver of Forms (Wâhib al-sowar): the Angel who, with the permission of his Lord, the Absolute Giver (Wahhâb), imparts to the soul the Forms or Ideas of knowledge. So it is written in that verse of the all-wise Book, the Quran, where the Angel addresses Maryam: “I am the messenger of your Lord, sent to give you a holy son” (19:19).
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00247

Mîr Dâmâd draws a further symbolic lesson from the legal status of rizâ'. The new kinship, with all its consequences, between a child and a woman who nurses the child without being its mother is legally established only when the child has been fed by her at least ten times. Likewise, the first stage of “intellectual or spiritual nursing” (rizâ' 'aqlânî) cannot be regarded as complete until the soul has assimilated the knowledge of the Ten Degrees distributed across the two hierarchies of Origin and Return—the two hemispheres, as it were, of the order of being (nizâm al-wojûd).
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00248

The whole Avicennian doctrine of the Intelligences is thus embraced by this double allusion. There are the Ten angelic Intelligences, marking the stages through which being proceeds, each giving rise to a world. The last of these is our own “Active Intelligence,” the Intelligence of humanity, the Holy Spirit: Angel of Knowledge, of the Annunciation, and of Revelation. In reality, however, all Ten are active Intelligences, and the Way of Return passes through successive elevations and teachings (tarbiyat), each presided over by one of them. This is also the spiritual initiation imparted in the long prologue to the Mi'râj-Nâmeh (Book of the Heavenly Ascent) attributed to Avicenna.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00249

These few pages, which bring such remarkable ta'wîl to the provisions of religious law, already reveal what Avicennianism means as Mîr Dâmâd lives it. By showing how a “kinship” is formed between the human soul, the “spiritual child,” and the angelic Intelligences, they confirm a feeling Avicenna himself expressed in his marginal notes on the so-called Theology of Aristotle: “The Active Intelligences,” he writes, “adorn and perfect the soul, which is like their child; for the soul’s intellectual nature is not given together with its substance, but is acquired.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00250

Elsewhere, we have had occasion to emphasize the warmth of feeling implicit in the relationship between the soul and the angelic Intelligences. This “angelic education,” flowing from Avicenna’s cosmology, is itself enough to guard us against interpreting Avicennianism in a one-sided rationalist manner. The bond between a child and its parent is precisely the relationship now expressed in Mîr Dâmâd’s own terms.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00251

The setting becomes richer still through the part played by the central figure of Avicenna’s theory of knowledge: the Active Intelligence, the Giver of Forms. It confirms our conviction that when our philosophers, through ta'wîl, “lead back” the Active Intelligence ('Aql fa''âl) to the Holy Spirit (Rûh al-Qods), they are very far from reducing spirit to intellect. Quite the reverse is true. Already in Avicenna, this movement back to the Holy Spirit shapes the mystical traveler’s personal relationship with his guide in the spiritual world, Hayy ibn Yaqzân.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00252

The identification of the Active Intelligence with the Holy Spirit—that is, in the language of Quranic theology, with Gabriel, the Archangel of the Annunciation—is anything but artificial. As we have just seen, it governs Mîr Dâmâd’s entire vision of the “spiritual birth” to which the philosopher’s very vocation calls him. This vocation can be fulfilled only because the Angel of the Annunciation and the “Giver of Forms” (wâhib al-sowar, Dator Formarum) are one and the same.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00253

Here this identity makes possible a mystical experience so genuine at its core that it immediately meets an archetypal theme: the divine birth within the soul, the human soul called to become the “mother of God,” as Meister Eckhart puts it. The same theme is expressed in the celebrated couplet of Angelus Silesius: “What good is it to me, Gabriel, that you greet Mary, if you have no such message for me?” The experience Mîr Dâmâd lived and expressed so briefly belongs to this same type of mystical experience.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00254

The spiritual fact of decisive importance is that his soul’s union with the Active Intelligence places the philosopher-mystic in Maryam’s own position before the Angel who is the Holy Spirit. In both cases, the Angel’s message is received in the same way, as expressed in the Quranic verse of the Annunciation (19:19). Here, it seems, we have an unanswerable personal testimony to the meaning of Avicennianism: it is more than a philosophical doctrine; it is a form of spiritual life. And it is moving that this testimony should come to us, six centuries after Avicenna, from the master of the School of Isfahan, Magister tertius.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00255

Mîr Dâmâd’s statements about the sage’s “theosophic” goal—the full realization of divine wisdom—are entirely consistent with this understanding. Ashkevarî also records the conclusion of the Zawâbit, which agrees word for word with statements found in the Book of Celestial Dewdrops; these, in turn, come almost literally from Sohrawardî.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00256

“The soul,” Mîr Dâmâd writes, “must become capable of combining contemplation of the world of Mysteries with the vision of the sensible world: capable of shedding its body, of loosening the knots in the ropes of physical nature, so that it may ascend to the spiritual world and unite with the archangelic Intelligences, whose Orient shines upon it (moshriqa) with the radiance of their illuminations (ishrâqât). No one truly takes a place among the sages until he has acquired the practiced ability to cast off his body, until it has become for him like a tunic that he puts on at one moment and removes at another.” Word for word, this is what we read in Sohrawardî.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00257

These reflections form the spiritual setting in which Ashkevarî invites us to understand the two “confessions of ecstasy” that we shall now read. The broad outlines of this setting already reveal what we have called Illuminationist Avicennism.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00258

The two accounts bring the nature of the spiritual experience into sharper focus, showing the specifically Shiite character of each. They demonstrate that when Mîr Dâmâd embraced Sohrawardî’s idea of a “metaphysics of ecstasy,” he was speaking from his own experience. He took care to record the dates of both spiritual events, which occurred roughly twelve years apart. The first took place in 1011 AH (1602–1603 CE): his vision in the mosque at Qom, whose imagery has since become established in Shiite devotion.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00259

The second occurred in 1023 AH (1614 CE), and its character is quite different. Although the two experiences are inwardly connected, their visionary imagery is distinct. The first reveals the whole inner world of a devout Shiite: the sudden appearance, upon the illuminated mirror of his soul, of figures he loves and reveres in the secrecy of his heart.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00260

The second gives us Mîr Dâmâd’s personal, experiential confirmation of the Avicennian vision of the cosmos, brought to incandescence in a visionary state. Whereas the second account survives in several transcriptions, the vision in the mosque at Qom is known to us, so far, only through Ashkevarî’s complete quotation of it, unfortunately without any indication of his source.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00261

During the “month of God”—that is, Ramadan—in the year 1011 AH (1601 CE), Mîr Dâmâd, then presumably in the fullness of his youth and already settled for some years in Isfahan, was staying in Qom. This was the protected holy city of the members of the Prophet’s Household (Ahl al-Bayt), Qom the Well-Guarded (Qomm al-mahrûsa). He had taken refuge there, he tells us, from the troubles of the time.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00262

One day, after the afternoon prayer, he lingered in the mosque. He remained kneeling where he had prayed, seated back upon his heels, still facing the direction of prayer, the qibla. Drowsiness gradually overcame him, and suddenly he felt himself swept away:
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00263
“Then,” he says, “I saw before me a radiant, translucent light (nûr sha'sha'ânî), shining with extraordinary splendor. It appeared in the form of a human figure lying on its right side.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00264

“I also saw another figure, sublime in appearance, majestic beyond measure in the beauty of its shimmering radiance and the brightness of the light spreading all around it. This second figure was seated behind the one lying down. It was as though I knew instinctively—or as though someone had told me—that the reclining figure was our Master, the Commander of the Faithful, while the figure seated behind him was our Lord the Prophet.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00265

“I was kneeling, seated upon my heels, directly opposite the reclining figure, facing him at the level of his chest. And then I saw him—the Imam, may God’s prayers and peace be upon him—honor me with a smile. He passed his blessed hand over my forehead, my cheek, and my chin, as though bringing me good news, dispelling my sadness, overcoming my disbelief, and shaking grief and desolation from my soul.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00266
The mystic then gathers the full attention of his inner faculties, but hears the Imam instructing him:
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00267

“Recite these words: Mohammad, the Prophet of God, is before me. Fâtima, the Daughter of the Prophet of God, is above me, over my head. The Commander of the Faithful, 'Alî ibn Abî-Tâlib, is at my right.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00268

“Hasan and Hosayn; 'Alî (Zayn al-'Âbidîn); Mohammad (Bâqir); Ja'far (Sâdiq); Mûsâ (Kâzim); 'Alî (Rezâ); Mohammad (Taqî); 'Alî (Naqî); Hasan ('Askarî); and the Guarantor, the Awaited One—all my Imams—are at my left. Abu Dharr, Salmân, Miqdâd, Hodhayfa, and 'Ammâr, the Companions of the Prophet, are behind me. The angels are all around me. And God, my Lord, encompasses me and is my guardian.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00269

Having introduced the visionary to this recitation, which establishes a complete spiritual world—the Twelve Imams and the Five Companions arranged as though for the celebration of a solemn inward liturgy—the Imam makes his disciple repeat the formula that gives shape to this inner vision. He repeats it once, then a second time, and again and again, until he knows it perfectly by heart. Only when this newly formed structure has taken firm root in his consciousness does Mîr Dâmâd awaken.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00270

“I shall long for that vision,” he concludes, “until the Day of Resurrection.” At the heart of this ecstatic experience was a supernatural initiation into a form of prayer whose deepest meaning lies in the integration of the soul and spirit into a complete whole. Such an experience calls for a fuller analysis than we can offer here, but we may at least indicate what seem to us its essential features. It should be compared with Haydar Âmolî’s vision beneath the night sky of Baghdad (above, Book IV, Chapter I, §4).
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00271

The complete image of Mîr Dâmâd’s vision in the mosque at Qom is arranged like a mandala, a symbolic pattern organized around a center, its outer boundary formed by the encircling angels. At the center stands the visionary himself. Around him are four groups: the Prophet; the First Imam; the eleven remaining Imams, ending with the Hidden Imam, the Awaited One; and finally the Prophet’s Companions.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00272

Rising above the entire arrangement, directly over the mystic’s head—and thus above the field of his consciousness—is the person of Fâtima. Every condition of the symbolism of the center seems to be present, allowing us to grasp the significance of this ecstatic experience. It marks the resolution of a long process of inward maturation, one that must have involved severe spiritual trials.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00273

The mystic has now truly reached the Center—his own center. In doing so, he has gained access to his own wholeness, the experience of integration: he recognizes the Self that encompasses him (mohît), yet remains beyond ordinary consciousness, on the far side of the boundary—the angelic crown—that both defines and surrounds him.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00274

Similarly, in Haydar Âmolî’s vision, the mystic’s Self is represented by the empty center of a rectangular figure. This encounter with the Self must not be confused with a dissolution into something impersonal, as though it were the opposite of an encounter with the supreme personal God. No one has ever seen God, or the Self.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00275

Yet their revelation takes shape through deeply personal symbols, within an encounter that is, above all, a dialogue. Mîr Dâmâd is surrounded by those who belong to him, and to whom he himself belongs. Fâtima’s commanding position is significant. Here she appears as Anima-Sophia, the soul as Wisdom, the symbol of personal wholeness.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00276

We shall see again that she stands at the heart of a distinctively Shiite understanding of divine Wisdom, while the supreme God remains invisible, beyond them all (min warâ'ihim), in an untouched transcendence that will give rise to the entire Ismaili doctrine of angels.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00277

In its structure, Mîr Dâmâd’s vision in the mosque at Qom might be compared with the ecstasy of Hermes, which culminates in the hymn: “Powers within me, sing the One and the All; sing in harmony with my will” (Corpus Hermeticum, XIII, 18). We might also compare it with the vision of Hermas (Similitude, X), who, accompanied by twelve young women representing twelve Holy Spirits, spends the night keeping watch near the Tower, awaiting the appearance at dawn of the “magnificent Angel.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00278

In each case, the vision brings together all the “powers of the soul”: presences dwelling within the soul, which an “angelic education” gradually makes familiar to the mystic’s consciousness. They bear the imprint of his origin and spiritual lineage. They are the very being of his being. These comparisons can only be suggested in passing.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00279

What matters here is that, in Mîr Dâmâd’s first confession of ecstasy, we encounter a specifically Imami—that is, Twelver Shiite—form of the experience of integration. In it, the fullness of being begins to reveal itself through the manifestation of the pleroma, the complete spiritual world experienced as an all-embracing Presence. Its distinctive features disclose the images and hopes that remain silently alive and active within the fervor of Shiite devotion.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd

3. Exaltation in Solitude
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00280

The second “confession of ecstasy” concerns a spiritual experience that came to Mîr Dâmâd some twelve years later (1023 AH / 1614 CE). The circumstances had changed. He was now in Isfahan; he had become a master, and his inner experience had deepened. This vision would come to him not in a mosque, but in solitude, during a private retreat.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00281

Hence our choice of a phrase borrowed from Barrès, which we earlier applied to Isfahan itself: “exaltation in solitude.” Building upon what we have learned about the spiritual setting of these visions, we shall show—and this will be the conclusion of the chapter—how this ecstasy puts its final stamp upon Mîr Dâmâd’s Avicennism, transforming it into a visionary experience.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00282

But first, the very date of the event offers a precious clue to its specifically Shiite character, confirming what the first account has already taught us. There can be little doubt that this narrative of ecstasy made a profound impression not only upon Mîr Dâmâd’s immediate disciples, as Ashkevarî’s careful transcription shows, but also upon later admirers whose intellectual outlook sometimes differed sharply from his own.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00283

The great theologian Majlisî, for example, included a transcription in his monumental encyclopedia. All these readers, from different perspectives, must have been struck by the living example of a master whose personal experience demonstrated the primacy of spiritual realization over purely theoretical knowledge.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00284

We must therefore begin with the date: Friday, 14 Sha'bân, in the year 1023 of the Hegira (1614 CE), eighteen years before Mîr Dâmâd’s death, when he must have been in the full strength of maturity. As in the earlier account, his care in recording the exact date—as someone today might do in a private diary—confirms the psychological significance of what he had undergone. He wished to preserve, in a brief account, the memory of an experience that had shaken his entire being.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00285

It was brought about by the recitation of a dhikr, a meditative invocation of God, centered upon two divine names: al-Ghanî, the One who is sufficient unto Himself, and al-Moghnî, the One who grants sufficiency and makes up for all that is lacking. The meaning contained in these names would suddenly transform Avicennian cosmology into an intensely dramatic vision.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00286

Yet if we consider the particular day on which Mîr Dâmâd chose to perform this dhikr, we discover that the elevation of Avicennian philosophy into visionary experience bears an unmistakably Shiite imprint.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00287

Indeed, the date itself announces the meaning and significance of the ecstasy, once we recognize the wealth of associations it would have carried for anyone formed within Shiite religious life, whatever branch of Shiism they belonged to. The special excellence of the month of Sha'bân, and of the spiritual exercises chosen for its observance, are familiar themes of practical theology.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00288

But the sacred power of this month reaches its height during the night between the fourteenth and fifteenth days, the night that divides the month into two halves. Religious traditions and liturgical prescriptions recommend particular prayers and spiritual exercises for its observance.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00289

Above all, its special significance lies in the belief that it marks the birth, in 255 AH (869 CE), of the Imam of our time: the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam, knowledge of whom is a saving spiritual knowledge, and whose eventual reappearance is to bring about the transfiguration of the world. Long before this, however, a traditional report (khabar) attributed to the Fifth Imam, Mohammad Bâqir (d. 115 AH / 733 CE), had expressed the sacred meaning of this mystical night in the following terms:
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00290

“When someone asked Imam Bâqir—peace be upon him—about the excellence of the night of mid-Sha'bân, he replied: ‘It is the most exalted of nights after the Night of Destiny (Laylat al-Qadr). On this night, God bestows His grace upon His worshippers and forgives them in His mercy. Make every effort, then, to draw near to God in intimacy on this night.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00291

“For this is the night concerning which God has sworn to Himself that He will not send away empty-handed anyone who calls upon Him, provided that person does not ask Him to sanction a transgression. ‘It is a Night that God established on our account and for our sake, we who are the members of the Prophet’s Household (Ahl al-Bayt), as a counterpart to the Night of Destiny established for our Prophet.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00292

“‘Devote yourselves, therefore, to invocation and the praise of God. Whoever glorifies God a hundred times on this Night will receive forgiveness for all their faults, and God will provide for their needs both in this world and in the world to come.’”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00293

The Ismaili traditions place particular emphasis on the inward meaning of this Night. A disciple asks why one sometimes hears of the excellence of the day (yawm) of mid-Sha'bân, when the saying attributed to the Prophet speaks of the night, not the day. The answer is that day and night here symbolize the respective positions of the Prophet and the Imam. The Prophet declared, “Sha'bân is my month,” referring to his prophetic mission, the Risâlat.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00294

But his emphasis on the night of mid-Sha'bân points to the exalted rank of our Master, the Commander of the Faithful. The Imam is the Night, for he possesses the ta'wîl: the spiritual interpretation that discloses the hidden meaning (bâtin) of revelation. The Prophet, by contrast, occupies the rank of the Day, for he proclaims its outward wording and apparent meaning (zâhir) through the revelation itself (tanzîl).
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00295

Religion contains both an outward and an inward dimension. The Prophet’s task was to reveal the outward dimension, while the other half—the inward meaning—was entrusted to his spiritual heir (wasî), the Imam. The Prophet therefore designated the Imam’s position symbolically as the “Night of the Half”: he is the guardian of the ta'wîl, the secret and hidden half of religion understood in its fullness. This is the meaning of the special excellence of the night of mid-Sha'bân.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00296

Among the Nusayri Shiites, moreover, the ritual and appointed readings for this same night are particularly elaborate. Here another feature comes into focus: the capacity to perceive each day, each month, as a “person.” This is not an allegorical device, but a way of understanding being itself, grounded in the visionary perception of archetypal persons.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00297

Thus, for example, the thirty days and thirty nights of Ramadan each have their own archetypal person: thirty male figures for the days, thirty female figures for the nights. The archetypal person of the Night of Destiny (Laylat al-Qadr) is Fâtima the Creator (Fâtir, in its masculine form). This conception belongs to a whole Shiite tradition concerning divine Wisdom, a sophiology, of which Louis Massignon first brought to light a text of extraordinary significance: Fâtima understood as Initiation itself.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00298

Fâtima is likewise perceived as the archetypal person of the night of mid-Sha'bân. Only a few pages ago, we saw her as the Figure presiding over the entire field of Mîr Dâmâd’s vision in the mosque at Qom, just as she presided over Haydar Âmolî’s vision beneath the night sky of Baghdad.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00299

Taken together, these indications allow us to glimpse the background of consciousness and of the deeper consciousness beyond it against which the precise date of Mîr Dâmâd’s second confession of ecstasy stands out. Which of his retreats was he staying in? Perhaps somewhere near Isfahan, on the banks of the Zendeh-Rûd? One would like to picture the setting.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00300

But what matters is the date: 14 Sha'bân. Although he does not tell us the hour, this was the day immediately preceding the most sacred night, that of the fourteenth to the fifteenth. Shiite ta'wîl has now shown us the profound meaning of this Day and this Night.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00301

The fourteenth day announces the imminent arrival of the night containing the Imam’s secret: the night that marks the dividing line between tanzîl, the outward revelation, and ta'wîl, the passage beyond its letter into its inward meaning. This passage beyond the letter is an exegesis—in the word’s original sense, a leading out, an exodus. For Mîr Dâmâd, this exegesis had become ekstasis, a standing outside oneself: the great Exodus spoken of by Sohrawardî, which Mîr Dâmâd, taking up the very words of the master of Ishrâq, had proposed as the goal of the mystical sage.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00302

Thus the date is far more than a chronological indication placing the event within historical time. The night of mid-Sha'bân is itself sacred, liturgical time: a revelation of the holy within time. It is the time of this ecstasy, an irruption of what lies beyond history. The spiritual and psychological event takes its distinctive form from the sacred date on which it occurred.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00303

Some years ago we published a critical edition of the short Arabic text containing this confession of ecstasy. We reproduce our translation here. It will give us the opportunity to recall, in conclusion, the central lesson we have sought to draw from Mîr Dâmâd’s two confessions. Both may now take their rightful place within the study of spiritual experience to which they belong.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00304

Epistle of Mohammad Bâqir (Mîr Dâmâd), recounting his ecstasy in the world of the Malakût. May God perpetuate the glory of its author! In the name of God, the Merciful, the All-Merciful. All glory belongs to the Lord of the worlds. May His blessings rest upon our lord Mohammad and the members of his Household, the Immaculate Ones.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00305

One day in the course of this present month—Friday, the fourteenth of the exalted Sha'bân, the month of the Prophet of God, in the year 1023 of his most holy Hegira—I was in one of my places of retreat, absorbed in meditation upon my Lord, multiplying my inward invocations and repetitions of His Name: “The One Who Is Sufficient unto Himself.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00306

I went on repeating without ceasing: “O You who are sufficient unto Yourself! O You who make all things sufficient!” I became oblivious to every concern except the desire to penetrate more deeply into the sanctuary of His Mystery and to feel myself dissolve within the radiance of His Light.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00307

Suddenly it was as though the lightning flash of a divine ecstasy came rushing upon me and tore me from the dwelling of my body. I broke the rings that held fast the nets of sensory perception; I untied the knots of the net of physical nature. I began to take flight on the wing of awestruck wonder, into the heaven of the angelic world—the Malakût—of True Reality.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00308

It was as though I had been stripped of my body and had left my familiar dwelling behind; as though I had polished the blade of my thought and been drawn from the sheath of my body; as though I had folded the expanse of time back upon itself and reached the world of eternity.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00309

And suddenly I found myself in the City of Being, among the archetypes of all the peoples who make up the harmony of the cosmos: beings that are primordial and beings that undergo change; divine and natural beings; heavenly and material beings; beings that endure and beings that exist in time.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00310

There were the peoples of Unbelief and those of Faith, the nations of Ignorance and those of Islam; those who advance and those who fall behind; those who came before and those who follow after, throughout all the ages of the past and all the ages yet to come.
